read:memory-model.checked:
I read all three files in full. c5-device-part.cu stops at line 545, which is the first comment line of k_reader. A diff shows its lines 1-545 are identical to /home/jetson/src/bpftime-gpu-work/proto/hashdesign/r2/src/c5.cu lines 1-545. I therefore checked k_reader in that file, lines 548-613, cited below as src/c5.cu. Nothing was run on the GPU and nothing was edited.

PRECONDITIONS
(a) Mixed-size races (8.7.2: "The axioms in the memory consistency model do not apply if a PTX program contains one or more mixed-size data-races."). The only access narrower than 64 bits is the outcome byte store at 536. Each thread writes its own byte in a separate allocation. Every other access is a 64-bit access to the same address, so there is no mixed-size race.
(b) Proxies (8.6). dir, rows and ctl are reached only through to_global of the one cudaMalloc pointer (487-494). Both grids therefore use the same virtual address through the generic proxy, and no alias fence is needed.
(c) Scope (8.5). Every operation is .gpu. k_reader is another grid on the same device: ".gpu ... This also includes other kernel grids invoked by the host program on the same compute device."
(d) Initial values. The memset and memcpy writes, including prefill, come before every kernel operation through API synchronization: "Start of a CUDA API call to enqueue a task synchronizes with start of the task." and "Start of a CUDA kernel synchronizes with start of all threads in the kernel." By 8.10.1 they are first in coherence order.

RELIANCES AND VERDICTS
1. One CAS winner per slot, and the key never changes (447; the only later writes are 455/469). FOLLOWS. CAS and st.release are both strong .gpu, so they are morally strong and ordered in coherence (8.9.6: "Two overlapping write operations are related in coherence order if they are morally strong..."). 8.10.3 forbids two CASes from 0 both writing.
2. Rows are unique, and exactly max_entries adds return a value below max (452). FOLLOWS. The adds are pairwise morally strong RMWs, so by 8.10.3 and 8.10.5 each reads its predecessor in coherence order.
3. Precheck with FAULT 0 (429 ld.acquire, 434 re-read). FOLLOWS.
- Each add is atom.acq_rel, so it is a release pattern ("A release operation on M"). That release covers the winner's CAS at 447: "only affects operations occurring in program order before the first instruction in that pattern".
- If 429 reads v >= max, each of the first v adds reaches 429 in observation order through the chain of adds ("For some atomic operation Z, W precedes Z and Z precedes R in observation order."). Each of them synchronizes with 429 (8.9.4).
- Case (a): K's successful claimant took the slot that 434 re-reads. Its CAS precedes 434 in causality, so by 8.10.6 the re-read cannot return the initial 0.
- Case (b): the claimant passed that slot and claimed a later one. It passed only after reading the slot non-empty, at 411 or through a failed CAS at 447; call that read Z. Z comes before 434 in base causality: Z, then (program order) the claimant's add, which synchronizes with 429, then (program order) 434. Z and 434 use the same address. By "For some operation Z, X precedes Z in observation order, and Z precedes Y in proxy-preserved base causality order.", the write that Z read precedes 434 in causality, so 434 cannot return 0.
- Otherwise the claimant's add comes after the add that 429 read in coherence order. It returns a value >= max and publishes refused, so K never becomes live.
- FAULT 5 lacks this protection because the walk's read at 411 comes before the acquire ("only affects operations occurring in program order after the last instruction in that pattern").
- Prefill == max: the count and headers come from cudaMemcpy and are first in causality. FOLLOWS.
4. Acquire half of 452. NOTHING RELIES ON IT. After its add the winner reads no shared state; it only does red at 464 and the publish.
5. Publish at 469 to k_reader (src/c5.cu 568 ld.relaxed, 569 fence.acq_rel, 581 shard loads). FOLLOWS, subject to finding 4.
- The red at 464 comes before 469 in program order, and 568 reading the publish is observation order.
- The path from 464 to 581 is proxy-preserved (same address, generic proxy).
- 8.10.6 forbids reading the memset 0, so the row sum at 583 is >= 1. This does not depend on red being strong.
- Non-decreasing sums (592) follow from 8.10.5, subject to finding 3.
6. Waiters' relaxed loads (273) and the HIT path (246, 516) need no acquire. EEXIST returns no data, and a HIT only adds atomically into rows zeroed before launch. The key cannot change while a thread waits (C_KEY_CHANGED stays 0) by rule 1 and 8.10.5. Refused leading to E2BIG is backed, because refused is published only after an add returned >= max. Whether these loads see the write in time is finding 1.
7. After EEXIST_LIVE or EEXIST_WAITED, the thread's own lookup at 526 is non-NULL. FOLLOWS from 8.10.5: the same thread re-reads slots it already saw non-empty, 0 is first in coherence, and keys are fixed.
8. Two slots for one key. EXCLUDED by rules 1 and 3, since a thread passes a slot only after reading it non-empty with a different key.
9. full_directory (324). When it reads a count >= max, E2BIG is backed as in rule 3. When the bound runs out (328-330), nothing observed backs it (finding 1).
10. Across launches. FOLLOWS: "Completion of a task enqueued in a CUDA stream synchronizes with the start of the following task in the same stream, if any.", together with the observation clause for chain slots.
11. k_reader's exit test (src/c5.cu 562) is relaxed; it only ends the loop.

SUMMARY
Under the model, no GPU-side scenario breaks CONTRACT.md. All four findings are doc-gap: (1) visibility within one launch depends on hardware; (2) the CPU reader is not covered by the .gpu scope; (3) red has no qualifier; (4) the wording for fence.acq_rel.

findings.title: Visibility within one launch and the contract's real-time clauses do not follow from chapter 8 (depends on hardware)
findings.scenario:
Threads X and Y run in the same k_ops launch with the same key K (with the default 64 keys, many threads share a key).
1. X's lookup returns NULL. X's insert reads slot a as empty (411) and reads count 0 < max (429). Its CAS wins (447), its add returns 0 (452), it does red on rows[0*256+sx] (464), publishes st.release live(K, row 0) (469) and returns OC_WON.
2. Later in wall-clock time (globaltimer), Y starts. Y's lookup does ld.relaxed of slot a (246). No release/acquire pattern or observation order links that load to X's st.release, so chapter 8 lets it return the memset value 0, and lookup returns NULL at 248-249.
3. Y then inserts. Its CAS at a must fail (8.10.3: only one CAS on a writes) and returns live(K). This takes the lost-to-same-key path, the wait sees live, and the outcome is OC_EEXIST_WAITED. The second lookup at 526 then finds K by 8.10.5.
4. The model has no progress clause anywhere. The waiter's ld.relaxed at 273 may keep returning claiming(K) for the whole bound even after the publish, giving OC_EEXIST_UNSTABLE. full_directory's ld.acquire at 324 may keep returning a count below max, so 328-330 return E2BIG without having observed anything that shows the map full.
findings.consequence: Within one launch, chapter 8 does not give CONTRACT 9-10 ("a key inserted before the lookup started must be found") or 13-14 ("consistent with real time"). They hold only if the hardware makes a .gpu store visible to later .gpu loads within bounded time; on sm_87 that presumably means through L2, which is hardware behaviour outside the document. Across launches in stream sA they do follow, through API synchronization. Y's case is recorded as an EEXIST outcome, the same code a genuine race produces, so the stress test cannot tell the two apart. Two things also rest on hardware timing rather than the model: the rate of unstable waits, and the E2BIG at 328-330. The documented deviation names only EEXIST, so it does not cover that E2BIG.
findings.doc_basis: 8 intro: "In the absence of any constraint, each read operation returns the value committed by some write operation to the same memory location, including the initial write to that memory location." The only eventual-visibility text in the chapter is 8.6.1, and it covers only cross-proxy access: "Strong modifications through generic-proxy, ... eventually become observable by strong accesses to the same location performed via a different proxy in that list". The chapter never mentions real time. For launches in the same stream: "Completion of a task enqueued in a CUDA stream synchronizes with the start of the following task in the same stream, if any."

findings.title: k_reader does not stand in for the CPU reader: every device-side release and add is .gpu-scoped
findings.lines: c5-device-part.cu 177-180 (st.release.gpu, used by publish 312-315 at 455 and 469); 173-176 with 464 and 516 (red, .gpu by default); CONTRACT.md 21-22 and 27; k_reader at src/c5.cu 568-581
findings.scenario:
Winner W adds 1 to rows[r*256+s] with red (464), then does st.release.gpu live(K, r) (469). A host thread H, the CPU reader named in CONTRACT 21, reads dir[a], sees live(K, r), and then reads row r's 256 shards.
1. H runs outside .gpu scope, so W's st.release.gpu and H's read cannot be morally strong.
2. Without that there is no observation order, no synchronizes-with, and no causality from W's red to H's shard reads. Chapter 8 then allows H to read the memset 0 from every shard and report K as live with value 0.
3. For the same reason the shard adds and H's reads are not morally strong, so CoRR does not apply, and H may see a shard decrease between polls.
How H actually reads is in none of the supplied files: host loads on mapped memory, or cudaMemcpyAsync on another stream, and with what scope. This scenario is conditional on that code.
findings.consequence: k_reader runs as another grid on the same device, inside .gpu. Its passing R_ZERO_SUM and R_DECREASE checks says nothing, under chapter 8, about the CPU reader the contract names. The contract's own target line ("scope .gpu") leaves that reader outside every guarantee. To fall under the model, the publish and the shard adds would need .sys scope (st.release.sys, or fence.acq_rel.sys before the publish, and red.relaxed.sys), and the CPU side would need an acquire. 8.1.1 also warns that atomicity at system scope may be limited.
findings.doc_basis: 8.5, .gpu: "The set of all threads in the current program executing on the same compute device as the current thread. This also includes other kernel grids invoked by the host program on the same compute device." .sys: "The set of all threads in the current program, including all kernel grids invoked by the host program on all compute devices, and all threads constituting the host program itself." 8.7: "each operation is strong and specifies a scope that includes the thread executing the other operation." 8.9.4 requires "the first operation in X and the last operation in Y are morally strong." 8.1.1: "When communicating with the host CPU, certain strong operations with system scope may not be performed atomically on some systems."

findings.title: Counter adds use red with no .sem and no scope; chapter 8 calls an operation strong only by its qualifier
findings.lines: c5-device-part.cu 173-176 (red.global.add.u64), used at 464 (winner) and 516 (HIT); k_reader at src/c5.cu 581, 590-592
findings.scenario:
The winner (464) and a HIT thread (516) both add to the same shard s = (smid&7)*32 + lane of K's row. Suppose these reds were not strong.
1. They would not be morally strong with each other, so 8.10.3 atomicity would not apply. Both could read 0 and write 1, and the shard would end at 1 instead of 2: one add lost.
2. They would also not be morally strong with k_reader's ld.relaxed at src/c5.cu:581. Then 8.10.5 (CoRR) would not stop a later poll from reading a smaller value than an earlier one (decrease++ at 592).
findings.consequence: Two properties follow only if red.global.add.u64 means relaxed at .gpu scope: no lost adds (CONTRACT 17 and the host's sum checks), and non-decreasing reader sums. That default is stated in the red instruction's description (chapter 9), not in the supplied chapter 8. The reader's sum >= 1 (src/c5.cu:583) does not depend on it, because 8.10.6 has no morally-strong condition. This is not a defect if the chapter-9 default holds. Writing red.relaxed.gpu.global.add.u64 would make the argument rest on chapter 8 alone.
findings.doc_basis: Table 20, strong operation: "A memory fence operation, or a memory operation with a .relaxed, .acquire, .release, .acq_rel, .volatile, or .mmio qualifier." 8.5: "Each strong operation must specify a scope". 8.10.3: "When an atomic operation A and a write W overlap and are morally strong". 8.10.5: "Within any set of overlapping memory operations that are pairwise morally strong". Partial support in 8.8: "atomic reductions conceptually perform a strong read".

findings.title: The reader's acquire pattern uses fence.acq_rel, but the acquire rule says "an acquire memory fence"
findings.scenario: W adds to rows[r*256+s] with red (464) and then publishes st.release live(K, r) (469). k_reader thread t does ld.relaxed of dir[a] and reads live(K, r) (src/c5.cu 568), then fence.acq_rel.gpu (569), then ld.relaxed of row r's shards (581). The sum >= 1 check at 583 needs "ld.relaxed; fence.acq_rel" to count as an acquire pattern, so that W's release pattern synchronizes with it. If it did not count, the shard loads could return the memset 0, and k_reader would see a live key with sum 0.
findings.consequence: The acquire bullet names only "an acquire memory fence", while the release bullet names "release or acquire-release memory fence". Chapter 8 never says that fence.acq_rel is an acquire fence. The text supports it indirectly: the MP litmus closes its acquire pattern with "F2: fence.sys;", and the SB litmus contrasts fence.sc with fence.acq_rel. But reading fence.sys as fence.acq_rel.sys is chapter-9 material. This is very likely fine. Using ld.acquire.gpu at src/c5.cu:568 instead would match "An acquire operation on M" directly and remove the question.
findings.doc_basis: 8.8: "Or a strong read on M followed by an acquire memory fence in program order" versus "Or a release or acquire-release memory fence followed by a strong write on M in program order". MP litmus: "If R1 observes W2, then the release pattern “F1; W2” synchronizes with the acquire pattern “R1; F2”." SB litmus: "If each fence.sc in this example were replaced by a fence.acq_rel instruction, then this outcome is not guaranteed."

read:bpf-semantics.checked:
I read all three files in full: CONTRACT.md, c5-device-part.cu (lines 1-545, FAULT == 0 path) and the chapter 8 text. I ran nothing on the GPU and edited no file. The review copy ends at line 545, before the body of k_reader. The host side is not in the file, so I could not check three things: that rows_cap >= max_entries, that the directory starts zeroed, and that BOUND starts at 0. The answers below assume all three.

(a) E2BIG while the map holds fewer than max_entries keys. Three paths decide E2BIG on a BOUND read of at least max: the precheck at 429, the refused winner at 452-458, and the full directory at 324. The saw-refused path at 417 and 305 implies BOUND >= max+1. BOUND changes only through the atom.acq_rel add at 452. Each add reads its immediate predecessor ("A reads any byte from a write W’ that precedes W in coherence order. A follows W in coherence order." cannot both exist, txt 401-402), so the add results are distinct: 0, 1, 2 and so on. That makes the first max adds reservations with r0 < max, made by distinct CAS winners, and those winners hold distinct keys because there is one slot per key (see b). So counted by reservations, these paths are correct. Counted by what lookup sees, they are not: finding 1. The full-directory timeout at 328-331 returns E2BIG without ever reading BOUND >= max: finding 2.

(b) E2BIG for a key that is in the map at some point of the call: none found. A slot leaves 0 only through the CAS at 447. Its later writes come only from the winner (455 or 469) and keep the same key. Because the CAS is atomic, every concurrent inserter of K stops at the same first slot, so K never sits in two slots.
- Precheck: suppose K's winner got r0 < max. Its add is then in the add chain that T2's acquire at 429 read from (observation order, txt 291-293). It synchronizes with that acquire (txt 305-307). The winner's earlier reads of the slots it passed, and its CAS, therefore precede T2's re-read at 434 in causality order (txt 357-360). By the Causality axiom (txt 488-489) the re-read cannot return 0, so the code takes the continue at 439. If the winner's add comes later in the chain, it gets r0 >= max and the slot is refused. FAULT 5 drops this re-read, which is why that control breaks.
- Refused paths: K's only slot is refused for good.
- Full directory: all S slots hold other keys, and a slot's key never changes.

(c) EEXIST that is not unstable, for a key that never gets in: none found. EEXIST_LIVE (416) and EEXIST_WAITED (277-279, 303-304) both need a read of live(K). Only K's winner writes live(K), at 469, and only after r0 < max. A lost CAS whose old value is live(K) or refused(K) also resolves correctly through wait_resolved. One case is out of lens: an unstable EEXIST can be returned for a key whose winner is later refused. It needs a stall of a full wait between 447 and 452, and it falls under the documented unstable deviation.

(d) NULL for a key whose insert completed before the lookup started.
- Same thread: SC per location (txt 463-467) rules this out after a win, after EEXIST_LIVE and after EEXIST_WAITED, so the C_EEXIST_THEN_NULL count must stay 0.
- Across threads, when "before" is a causality path: the lookup finds K. Every write that the inserter observed on K's chain, and its publish, precede the lookup's reads in causality order.
- When "before" means only wall-clock time: finding 3.
- Line 254 returns NULL for good if row >= rows_cap, and the win is then reported as OC_ANOM_ROW (466-467). FAULT 0 cannot reach this if rows_cap >= max_entries (host side, not visible).

(e) A key counted twice, or a count lost: none found. There is one slot per key, and only CAS winners reserve, so no key reserves twice. Refused adds push BOUND up but always get r0 >= max and never take a row. Every winner publishes. Rows are distinct values of r0. Value changes are atomic red adds. When k_ops gets EEXIST it does not add; that is the bpf lookup-then-NOEXIST idiom, not a protocol fault.

Out of lens (cost only): refused slots are permanent, one per distinct key that passed the precheck near the full point, and S >= 2*max does not bound how many there are. A start burst of at least S threads with distinct keys can therefore fill the directory: M live slots plus S-M refused. After that, every lookup of an absent key walks all S slots (260), and every insert of an absent key walks S slots and then goes through full_directory. The results stay correct.

findings.title: E2BIG counts a reserved key that lookup still returns NULL for: insert(K2)=E2BIG then lookup(K1)=NULL fits no one-at-a-time order
findings.lines: E2BIG paths: 429-436 (precheck), 452-458 (refused winner), 417-419 and 305-307 (saw refused), 324-326 (full directory). The key K1 is in flight between 452 and 469. lookup returns NULL on claiming at 251-252.
findings.scenario:
Setup: max_entries = M. Keys A1..A(M-1) are live. Only one other insert is in flight, T1's insert of K1.
1. T1 runs insert(K1). It reaches an empty slot s and its precheck at 429 reads BOUND = M-1. It wins the CAS at 447, so slot s holds (K1<<32)|1, which is claiming(K1). Its atom.acq_rel add at 452 returns r0 = M-1, so BOUND is now M. T1 has not yet run 464 or 469.
2. T2 runs insert(K2); K2 is absent. Its walk reaches an empty slot j. The ld_acquire at 429 reads M >= M. The re-read of j at 434 returns 0. It returns OC_E2BIG and counts C_E2BIG_PRECHECK.
3. T2 (or any thread that starts after T2's insert returned) runs lookup(K1). The walk from home(K1) reaches s. The doc guarantees this read is not 0: T2's acquire synchronized with T1's add, and the CAS comes before that add in T1's program order. The read returns claiming(K1), so line 252 returns NULL.
4. T1 publishes live(K1, M-1) at 469 and returns OC_WON.

Why no order fits: insert(K2)=E2BIG needs M keys in the map at its point. K2 is not one of them, so the only candidates are A1..A(M-1) plus K1, and K1 must already be in. lookup(K1) starts after insert(K2) returned, so its point comes later. Keys are never removed, so the lookup must find K1. It returned NULL.

This is a plain interleaving; no weak-memory reordering is needed. Per the doc the window can last even past T1's publish: T2's synchronization covers only what T1 did before the add, and the publish comes after it.

The other E2BIG paths give the same result:
- Refused winner: T4 wins a CAS for K4. Its add at 452 returns M, it publishes refused at 455 and returns E2BIG at 458. Then lookup(K1) returns NULL.
- Saw refused: T5 reads refused(K4) at 417 or 305 and returns E2BIG. Then lookup(K1) returns NULL.
- Full directory: 324 reads BOUND >= M. Then lookup(K1) returns NULL.
findings.consequence:
This breaks CONTRACT lines 11-14. For E2BIG the map counts reserved keys (the add at 452), but for lookup it counts only live ones (251-252). A bpf program that runs "if (update(K2, NOEXIST) == E2BIG) v = lookup(K1)" sees a full map and still misses K1.

The stress test cannot detect this. k_ops (510-534) has each thread look up and insert only its own key K, so C_EEXIST_THEN_NULL and the other counters never pair one key's E2BIG with another key's lookup.

There are two ways out:
- Change the contract: an E2BIG is judged against reserved keys, which include keys still being inserted, and a lookup may miss those keys.
- Change the code: a second counter, bumped after the publish at 469, gates every E2BIG path, with a bounded wait while that counter is below max_entries.

Aside, from unverified recall and outside the three files: Linux htab appears to take the element (freelist pop or count increment) before linking it, holding only the new key's bucket lock, while its lookups take no lock. If so, Linux has the same cross-bucket window, and the claim in CONTRACT line 14 that "each bucket is locked" gives this order only for operations on the same bucket. Either way, the code as written does not meet CONTRACT as written.
findings.doc_basis:
CONTRACT lines 11-14: "E2BIG if K is not in the map and the map holds max_entries keys" and "behave as if they happened one at a time in some order consistent with real time". CONTRACT line 15-16: "So keys are never removed."

PTX txt 305-307: "A release pattern X synchronizes with an acquire pattern Y, if a write operation in X precedes a read operation in Y in observation order, and the first operation in X and the last operation in Y are morally strong." This shows T2 is guaranteed to see the claim.

PTX txt 237-238: "Any memory synchronization established by a release pattern only affects operations occurring in program order before the first instruction in that pattern." T1's publish at 469 comes after its add at 452 in program order, so T2 is not guaranteed to see live.

findings.title: Full-directory timeout returns E2BIG without ever reading BOUND >= max_entries; CONTRACT does not list this deviation
findings.lines: 319-336, especially 328-331 (C_FULLDIR_UNSTABLE), reached from 480. The CAS winners are stalled between 447 and 452. The wait bound is set at 45.
findings.scenario:
Setup: max_entries = M and S = 2M, the minimum in CONTRACT. No slot is refused yet.
1. At least S-M+1 = M+1 threads with distinct keys pass the precheck (BOUND < M), win CAS at 447 on distinct slots, and have not yet run the add at 452. The remaining slots, at most M-1, are live or have already reserved.
2. T6 runs insert(K6); K6 is absent. Its walk sees all S slots non-empty with other keys (409-426), so line 480 calls full_directory.
3. Every ld_acquire at 324 reads BOUND < M. The requested sleeps add up to WAIT_BOUND_NS (100000, line 45). Lines 328-331 return OC_E2BIG.

Throughout T6's call fewer than M keys are reserved, and fewer than M are live.

This needs the M+1 claimers to stay stalled between two adjacent instructions for the whole wait. Chapter 8 says nothing about scheduling, progress or time, so whether that can happen is hardware behaviour beyond the document.

The code sets no time bound either. Line 45 calls the bound "requested nanosleep total", and line 89 tracks the actual globaltimer time separately (C_WAIT_MAX_REQ_NS vs C_WAIT_MAX_NS). The poll at 324 may also keep returning an older BOUND (no recency guarantee, txt 7-8). That matters only when BOUND in real time is still below M.

If any refused slot exists, BOUND was already at least M+1 in real time, and the E2BIG is right.
findings.consequence:
Here E2BIG comes back while the map holds fewer than max_entries keys at every point of the call. The answer is early rather than wrong for good: each of the M+1 stalled claimers will add, so M is reached later and no slot ever frees.

CONTRACT lines 18-20 document only the unstable EEXIST. This path is counted (C_FULLDIR_UNSTABLE) but not documented. Either add "E2BIG, unstable (full directory, bound ran out)" to CONTRACT's deviations, or judge the stress results with this counter expected to be 0.
findings.doc_basis:
CONTRACT lines 11-12: "E2BIG if K is not in the map and the map holds max_entries keys". CONTRACT lines 18-20: the only listed deviation is "it returns EEXIST, counted as \"unstable\"".

PTX txt 7-8: "In the absence of any constraint, each read operation returns the value committed by some write operation to the same memory location, including the initial write to that memory location." Nothing in chapter 8 bounds the time before the claimers' adds become visible.

findings.title: "Consistent with real time" is not provided by chapter 8: lookup finds a completed insert only when "before" is a causality path
findings.lines: 241-261 (ld_relaxed at 246, NULL at 249 and 252); publish at 469; inserter's walk reads at 411 and 447
findings.scenario:
1. T1 in CTA a runs insert(K). It wins, publishes live(K) at 469 with st.release, and returns OC_WON.
2. T3 in CTA b, in the same launch, starts lookup(K) later by wall clock (for example ordered by %globaltimer stamps). No release/acquire handoff, barrier or kernel boundary connects T1 to T3.
3. T3's ld_relaxed at 246, on slot s or on any slot before s on K's chain, has no causality order from T1's writes. No axiom stops it from returning claiming(K), which gives NULL at 252, or the initial 0, which gives NULL at 249.

When T1's insert does precede T3's lookup in causality order, through a release/acquire handoff or the next launch on the same stream (txt 310-311), the property holds:
- Each slot write W_j that T1 observed while walking (411, 434, or a failed CAS at 447) precedes T1's read in observation order. That read precedes T3's read of the same address in proxy-preserved base causality order. So W_j precedes T3's read in causality order (txt 357-360).
- T1's publish precedes T3's read directly.
- By the Causality axiom, T3 cannot read 0 or claiming(K), so the lookup returns K's pointer.

Within one thread the property follows from SC per location (txt 463-467).
findings.consequence:
Judged against wall-clock time, a NULL from lookup after an insert that finished earlier by wall clock is not excluded by the document. Whether it can happen depends on hardware behaviour beyond the document, such as coherence of .gpu-scope relaxed loads.

If the stress analysis judges the order by globaltimer stamps, it tests the hardware, not the design. The words "inserted before the lookup started" (CONTRACT line 9) and "consistent with real time" (line 14) should be read as "precedes in causality order". Under that reading the design meets them, as argued above. The CPU-side reader's notion of "before" needs the same definition.
findings.doc_basis:
PTX txt 7-8: "In the absence of any constraint, each read operation returns the value committed by some write operation to the same memory location, including the initial write to that memory location."

PTX txt 485-489: "Relations in communication order cannot contradict causality order. This constrains the set of candidate write operations that a read operation may read from:" and "If a write W precedes an overlapping read R in causality order, then for any byte accessed by both R and W, R cannot read from any write W’ that precedes W in coherence order."

PTX txt 358-360: "For some operation Z, X precedes Z in observation order, and Z precedes Y in proxy-preserved base causality order."

read:progress-capacity.checked:
Read CONTRACT.md, c5-device-part.cu (all 545 lines) and the chapter 8 text in full. I also grepped src/c5.cu, outside the three review files, only for the host sizing of S, logS and rows_cap. Lens: progress and capacity, FAULT == 0.

Termination:
- lookup (245) runs at most S iterations.
- In insert, every iteration does one of three things: returns, advances i together with n (425, 478), or takes the precheck `continue` (439), which advances neither. A walk of S slots therefore visits each slot exactly once.
- The `continue` terminates. Every slot access is strong, .gpu scoped and on the same .global address: ld.relaxed.gpu (131), atom.relaxed.gpu.cas (159), st.release.gpu (179). They are therefore pairwise morally strong (§8.7: "each operation is strong and specifies a scope that includes the thread executing the other operation"; same thread: "The operations are related in program order").
- §8.10.5 says "communication order cannot contradict program order" (CoRR). The host zeroing comes before every CAS in causality order: §8.9.4 "Completion of a task enqueued in a CUDA stream synchronizes with the start of the following task in the same stream" and "Start of a CUDA kernel synchronizes with start of all threads in the kernel", plus §8.10.1 Coherence.

Waits:
- wait_resolved (266-298) and full_directory (319-336) each run 53 nanosleeps. The sleep doubles from 64 to 2048 and then stays at 2048 until the requested total reaches 100288 ≥ 100000. That is 54 reads, and the u32 total cannot overflow.
- WAIT_BOUND_NS bounds the requested sleep total, not wall time. The actual nanosleep duration is not covered by chapter 8.
- An insert enters at most one wait, because after_wait returns.
- What a waiter returns: live gives EEXIST_WAITED, refused gives E2BIG, bound runs out gives EEXIST_UNSTABLE. full_directory always returns E2BIG.
- k_ops has no early exit before __syncthreads (538).

No permanent claiming slot: between the claim (447) and the publish (455/469) the code is straight-line, with no loop or wait. A slot stays claiming only if its winner stops running. Within a live context that means the kernel died, which kills the context and the device copy with it. That is runtime behaviour, not chapter 8.

- Each add at 452 follows a won CAS on a distinct slot that never empties again. By RMW atomicity (§8.10.3) one CAS wins per slot and the adds return distinct values. So count ≤ S ≤ 2^31; the u64 cannot overflow.

- Live slots ≤ max_entries, because rows are the distinct r0 < max.
- The 29-bit row field (253, 469) holds any r0 < max. Reaching max > 2^29 would need 2^29 × 256 × 8 B = 1 TiB of rows, so I checked it and it is not a finding.
- One key never gets two slots. A walker reaching K's slot either reads K (414) or loses the CAS to K (472). Any earlier slot that K's claimer passed was already won, so the walker's CAS there fails. Refused slots are therefore at most the number of distinct keys.

findings.title: Permanent refused slots can fill the whole directory; after that every absent-key lookup and insert walks all S slots
findings.lines: 429-441 and 447-458 (precheck, claim, reserve, refuse); 242-261 (lookup walk); 409-480 (insert walk); 319-326 (full_directory)
findings.scenario:
Setup: empty device copy, max_entries = 128, S = 256 (the host's sizing, src/c5.cu 746-751, outside the review files). 256 threads hold distinct absent keys, for example the host's one-key-per-thread mode.

Interleaving, which needs only concurrency and no weak memory behaviour:
1. Each thread reaches its first empty slot and runs the line-429 ld.acquire on the count before any of them reaches 452, so every one reads 0.
2. Each CAS at 447 wins a distinct slot. A loser at 476-478 moves on and prechecks again at the next empty slot, again reading 0.
3. All 256 slots are claimed, and the adds at 452 return 0..255.
4. r0 0..127 publish live (469); r0 128..255 publish refused (455).

Result:
- No slot is empty, and none ever will be again: nothing writes 0 to a slot, and keys are never removed (CONTRACT 15-16).
- From then on, for any key outside the 128 live ones:
  - lookup reads all 256 headers (245-259), bumps C_LOOKUP_FULLWALK and returns NULL.
  - In k_ops, insert reads all 256 headers again (409-479).
  - full_directory then reads the count once (324: 256 ≥ 128) and returns E2BIG.

Bounds:
- Refused slots ≤ S - max_entries, because live ≤ max_entries.
- Refused slots are also at most the number of threads sitting between 429 and 452 when the count crosses max_entries.
- How many is actually reached depends on timing and hardware. I did not observe it. The one-key-per-thread mode (1e6 distinct keys) can reach a full directory, but I have not seen it do so.
- Later launches in the same stream cannot add refused slots: their line-429 reads must return a count ≥ max. So occupancy freezes once a launch boundary follows the crossing.
findings.consequence:
Results stay correct: present keys are still found before S slots, and absent keys get NULL or E2BIG. The problem is capacity and cost.

- The sizing "at least twice max_entries" (CONTRACT 3-4) does not hold. Refused slots act as permanent tombstones, and the load factor can reach 1.0 for the life of the device copy.
- Each miss after the fill costs S relaxed global loads in lookup plus S in insert, plus one acquire. That is 512 loads at max 128, and about 65k at max 10240 (S 32768).
- bpf's full-map E2BIG is a constant-time count check.
- Short of a full fill, refused clusters lengthen the linear-probe runs for present keys as well. The expected miss length is about (1 + 1/(1-a)^2)/2: 2.5 at a = 0.5, 8.5 at 0.75, 50.5 at 0.9.
findings.doc_basis:
One winner per slot and distinct r0 values follow from §8.10.3: "When an atomic operation A and a write W overlap and are morally strong, then the following two communications cannot both exist in the same execution, for the set of bytes accessed by both A and W: A reads any byte from a write W' that precedes W in coherence order. A follows W in coherence order." (Litmus Test 1: "FINAL STATE: x == 2").

That occupancy freezes across launches follows from §8.9.4, "Completion of a task enqueued in a CUDA stream synchronizes with the start of the following task in the same stream" and "Start of a CUDA kernel synchronizes with start of all threads in the kernel", together with §8.10.6: "If a write W precedes an overlapping read R in causality order, then for any byte accessed by both R and W, R cannot read from any write W' that precedes W in coherence order."

findings.title: full_directory returns E2BIG when its bound runs out with count < max_entries: a second timeout outcome the contract does not document
findings.scenario:
Counting:
- The walk reaches 480 only after passing all S slots non-empty with a key other than K. Slots never empty again, so every slot has been won at 447.
- The winners that have run 452 number c, the count. So S - c winners have done their CAS but not yet their add.
- For 328 to fire, every one of the 54 reads at 324 must return c < max_entries. That means at least S - max_entries + 1 ≥ max_entries + 1 winners are parked between 447 and 452 for the whole wait.

Example: max 128, S 256. At least 129 winners stall. Thread T (new key K) walks 256 slots, sleeps 53 times, reads count < 128 every time, and returns OC_E2BIG, counted in C_FULLDIR_UNSTABLE. When the winners resume, the count reaches S ≥ 2·max, so the map does end up holding max_entries keys.

A stall like this depends on hardware and scheduling; chapter 8 says nothing about it.

The document alone also allows the 54 count reads to be stale even with every add done:
- The walk's header reads are ld.relaxed (246, 411).
- A relaxed header read followed by an ld.acquire of the count is not an acquire pattern, so the adds behind the live and refused headers T passed need not be visible at 324.
- In that variant the count really is ≥ S ≥ max, so E2BIG is right in substance and the counter just attributes it to the timeout. A nonzero C_FULLDIR_UNSTABLE therefore does not by itself show a premature E2BIG.
findings.consequence:
When T returns, the count shows fewer than max_entries reservations, yet T reports E2BIG. CONTRACT 11 allows E2BIG only when "the map holds max_entries keys". The documented deviation (18-20) covers only EEXIST after a bound.

In kind this path only widens a window the other E2BIG paths already have. Every E2BIG path (305-307, 417-419, 434-436, 454-458, 324-326) is keyed on the reservation count, which can reach max before the winners publish at 469.

I could not build a history whose wrong result belongs to this path alone. I therefore file it as a doc gap: the contract should name this outcome. Strictly against the contract text it is a violation, reachable only through the stall above.
findings.doc_basis:
Chapter 8 constrains only which write a read may return; it gives no bound on how long a thread may take between two of its own instructions: "In the absence of any constraint, each read operation returns the value committed by some write operation to the same memory location, including the initial write to that memory location."

The stale-count variant follows from §8.8, where the acquire pattern requires the same location: "Or a strong read on M followed by an acquire operation on M in program order".

The counting relies on RMW atomicity (§8.10.3, quoted in the first finding).

findings.title: The wait can run out on a claim that ends refused: EEXIST for a key that is never inserted, and lookup returns NULL permanently
findings.scenario:
Setup: max_entries = 48, count = 47.

1. Thread A (key K) reads count 47 at 429 and wins slot s at 447, which now holds claiming(K).
2. Thread C (key K2) adds at 452 first. The count goes from 47 to 48, and C gets row 47 and publishes live.
3. A is delayed between 447 and 452/455 for longer than the wait. This depends on hardware. One candidate is thread B sitting in A's warp under independent thread scheduling, where B's wait loop runs before A's tail; chapter 8 does not cover this.
4. Thread B (key K): lookup sees claiming(K) and returns NULL (251-252).
5. B's insert reads claiming(K) at 411/414 and goes to 421-422. wait_resolved reads claiming(K) 54 times across 53 sleeps and returns 0. after_wait then returns OC_EEXIST_UNSTABLE (309), and B's own lookup at 526 returns NULL.
6. A now adds: r0 = 48 ≥ 48, so it publishes refused(K) at 455 and returns E2BIG.

After this, K is never in the map. Every later lookup of K returns NULL (251-252), and every later insert of K gets E2BIG (417-419).
findings.consequence:
B got EEXIST for a key that is never inserted. The correct answer under CONTRACT 11 is E2BIG: K is not in the map, and the map holds max_entries keys.

The documented deviation (CONTRACT 18-20) does allow EEXIST after the bound. But its wording, "(the caller may then get NULL from lookup)", reads as transient, and here the NULL is permanent. A caller using the NOEXIST-then-lookup counter idiom gets EEXIST and then NULL forever, where it should get E2BIG. The contract should say that an unstable EEXIST may belong to a claim that ends refused.

Cost note for the same stall: if the claimer shares the waiter's warp, the waiter may spend the full bound each time. That bound is 100 µs of requested sleep; its wall-clock length depends on nanosleep, which chapter 8 does not cover.
findings.doc_basis: §8.5: "Note that the warp is not a scope; the CTA is the smallest collection of threads that qualifies as a scope in the memory consistency model." Chapter 8 contains no forward-progress guarantee for A. Nothing bounds when A's st.release at 455 becomes visible to B's ld.relaxed at 273; the only rule is that "each read operation returns the value committed by some write operation to the same memory location". So the document allows B to read claiming(K) for the whole bound.

findings.title: The device code relies on host preconditions it neither states nor checks: rows_cap ≥ max_entries, S == 1<<logS, logS ≥ 1
findings.scenario:
(a) rows_cap ≥ max_entries. Example: rows_cap = 32 and max_entries = 64.
- The 33rd winner gets r0 = 32 and skips the add (463-467, OC_ANOM_ROW), so K's value is never 1.
- It still publishes live (469).
- Every lookup of K then returns NULL (254-255), and later inserts of K get EEXIST_LIVE (415-416) followed by NULL.

(b) S == 1<<logS. home_slot (221) returns values below 2^logS, while the walk masks with S-1 (258, 424). If S < 2^logS, the first header read at 246/411 goes past the directory.

(c) logS ≥ 1. With logS = 0 (S = 1, which happens only when max_entries = 0), line 221 shifts a u64 by 64, which is undefined in C++.

The host (src/c5.cu 746-751, outside the review files) sets S to the smallest power of two ≥ 2·max_entries and rows_cap = S. So the stress test meets (a) and (b), and meets (c) for any max_entries ≥ 1.
findings.consequence: There is no wrong result in the stress test as configured. A later integration, such as bpftime map creation, that sizes rows below max_entries, or passes S and logS separately, would get silent permanent NULLs or out-of-bounds directory reads. These preconditions belong in CONTRACT.md or in device-side asserts.
